data.title: Binaries Masquerading as System Components Not Detected
data.summary:
Executables named and located to resemble legitimate operating system components ran
without detection, and were not distinguished from the genuine binaries by any control.
data.description:
Masquerading exploits the fact that both humans and rules commonly match on name and path
rather than on identity. An executable placed where an analyst expects a system binary,
with the name of one, passes casual review and frequently passes allow-list rules written
by path.

The genuine binaries are signed and present in protected locations, so the discrimination
is available — publisher and hash both distinguish them — but only where the control is
written that way. Path-based rules are easier to write and are what is usually found.

It also degrades response: during an investigation, the analyst's familiarity with system
process names works against them.
data.recommendation:
* Write application control rules against publisher and hash rather than path and filename.
* Alert on system binary names executing from paths other than their protected locations.
* Alert on unsigned executables running from user-writable directories.
data.short_recommendation: Base application control on publisher and hash, never on path.

attack_techniques.technique: T1036.005 — Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location
